The issue is clouded...'), reports only 'a short series of lexical items... which fit into the African lexical tone pattern', and gives final-syllable stress only for 'The African speakers -- not the English schooled West Cameroonian' with an 'especially those which end in high vowels /i/ and /u/' hedge, beside initial-stressed /ápsen/ /óda/ /áfta/; the supporting Bellama passage gives a two-tone H/L system with minimal pairs. …
3532.dq: The African speakers -- not the English schooled West Cameroonian -- place stress on the last syllable of a word especially those which end in high vowels /i/ and /u/. (Schneider 1963: 53). The modern account lumps word and phrase: 'final syllable of each word taken in isolation and of the sense group in connected speech' (Mbassi-Manga 1976 apud Menang 2008: 148, snippet).
3532.dloc: Schneider 1963 p. 53 = firststepsinwesk00schn (file read:); Bellama 1983 pp. iii-iv; Menang 2008 p. 148 and Ayafor & Green 2017 pp. 39-41 via Google Books
3532.prule: No word-stress rule of record. Schneider 1963 (p. 53) treats stress as unresolved and speaker-dependent: speakers without English schooling put stress on the last syllable of a word, 'especially' words ending in /i/ /u/, while English-schooled speakers keep English stress (initial-stressed /ápsen/ /óda/ /áfta/ on the same page); he also finds a set of lexical items with African-style lexical tone. The later descriptions code the language as a (reduced) two-tone H/L system with tonal minimal pairs (Bellama 1983 pp. iii-iv: bábà 'barber' / bàbá 'father', pópò 'proper' / pòpó 'pawpaw'; APiCS ch. 18 §4; Ayafor & Green 2017: 39 'reduced tone system'), with no English-type unstressed syllables and a slight final-syllable prominence (Mbassi-Manga 1976 as reported by Menang 2008: 148 and Ayafor & Green 2017: 41).
3532.srule: Not mentioned in Schneider 1963 (Unit Four Part Four 'Sounds: Stress and Tone in Wes-kos', pp. 53-54, read in full; nor pp. 7, 36). Later descriptions leave no separate secondary stress: 'each syllable is uttered with the same amount of strength, except the last syllable which receives slightly more energy' (Mbassi-Manga 1976 apud Menang 2008: 148, excerpt); Ayafor & Green 2017: 41 name 'primary and secondary stress' only to add 'since CPE does not have unstressed syllables in the way that English does' (excerpt; clause-initial words not visible).

3535.prule: Primary (strongest) stress falls on the first or the second syllable of the word; which of the two is fixed per root and is written with an accent in the dictionary (roots of inflecting words, and 2-3-syllable words that are not paroxytone); no rule computing the position from syllable count or weight is given, so the position is lexically listed within a left-edge two-syllable window.
3535.srule: A secondary (second-degree) stress falls on the word-final syllable; syllables between the main stress and the final syllable may carry tertiary stress or none, their position conditioned morphologically by the suffixes; when the main stress itself falls on the word-final syllable (e.g. monosyllabic 'da) the final secondary is eliminated (example: zi'taminanàarí). [The 1966 dictionary note only implies further weaker stresses ('la primera sílaba tónica... lleva más fuerza que las demás'; suffix accent 'casi constante') without placing them; its double-accented chóró, kápá, máká, gópogó, dáraná (p. 233) are consistent with the final-syllable secondary.]

El acento de los sufijos se observará en el Apéndice Notas Gramaticales y como es casi constante, no es necesario escribirlo. 3538.heavy: Stress is 'non-sensitive to syllabic weight' (Table 21, p. 126). Weight matters only for the separate high tone: a closed syllable (overt or underlying final consonant) in an even position to the right of the stressed syllable attracts the high tone; closed syllables in odd positions do not count (closed syllables 'are heavy only in even positions', p. 156).
3538.prule: Primary stress (realised as vowel lengthening; high pitch is a separate tone feature) is metrical and quantity-insensitive: disyllabic trochees are built from left to right, no degenerate feet, and the primary stress falls on the first syllable, the head of the leftmost foot. Fixed for every word of 2 and 3 syllables and for all non-predicates of any attested length; predicates of 4 syllables instead stress the head of the rightmost foot (syllable 3); in words of 5-7 syllables the first two syllables form their own prosodic unit whose head always carries a primary stress in predicates and non-predicates alike.
3538.srule: Secondary stress (vowel longer than unstressed, shorter than primary) on the head of every non-primary foot; feet are disyllabic trochees built left to right with no degenerate feet, so stresses fall on odd-numbered syllables from the left and a final odd syllable is unstressed. None in 2- and 3-syllable words ('The third syllable of trisyllabic words does not carry a secondary stress', p. 134); 4 syllables: non-predicates (»σ.σ)(«σ.σ), predicates («σ.σ)(»σ.σ); 5-7 syllables (Table 23): (»σ.σ)//(«σ.σ)σ, (»σ.σ)//(«σ.σ)(«σ.σ), (»σ.σ)//(«σ.σ)(«σ.σ)σ, the rightmost head optionally a second primary; certain CVC verbal suffixes in odd positions form their own foot in long predicates (§4.3.6).

This can be seen in the following examples: (129) Tetrasyllabic non-predicates: (»σ@.σ)(«σ.σ) baka=kama (»ba@.ka)(«ka.ma) ‘river=PLU’ ... (130) Tetra…
3538.tone: The author analyses the language as combining stress (vowel lengthening) with a separate high tone (no low tone; H vs unmarked). High tone goes on the rightmost prominent syllable (the primary-stressed syllable or a closed syllable in an even position to its right); the last syllable of words of 3+ syllables cannot carry it unless lexically marked; it is 'non-obligatory' and 'non-culminative' and in some trisyllabic/tetrasyllabic words ('uchíti 'dog', kuríki 'money', 'antánama 'scorpion') and a few suffixes it is lexical. Disyllables with a final consonant have stress on σ1 and H on σ2 (list (151)(i)). Shell (1950, 1986) analysed the high pitch as stress; Zariquiey argues stress (length) and tone (pitch) must be separated (pp. 168-169). Praat-measured; the author calls the account preliminary and words of 5+ syllables 'a very complex prosodic behaviour that I do not completely understand yet' (p. 140).

Stress is restricted to an initial three-syllable window, a typologically highly unusual pattern that has been predicted not to exist (Hulst 1999)" (p. 171). 3543.prule: Lexically contrastive stress confined to an initial three-syllable window: stress falls on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable of the word, never further right (minimal pairs ˈmúri 'basket' / muˈrí 'turtle'). Roots are lexically stressed (fixed 1st-, 2nd- or 3rd-syllable stress across paradigms, blocking morphological shifts) or unstressed; unstressed roots take default second-syllable stress with stress-neutral suffixes (rule (17), p. 151) and shift stress one syllable rightward with stress-shifting suffixes (onto the suffix after mono- and disyllabic roots, onto the root-final third syllable of trisyllabic roots).
3543.srule: None: 'There is no evidence for secondary stress in Choguita Rarámuri. That is, there is no impressionistic evidence of rhythmic prominence' (p. 135); 'Each prosodic word has a single main stress. There is no secondary stress (i.e., stress is non-iterative)' ((5a-b), p. 405).
3543.quote: [p. 43] Stress in Choguita Rarámuri is lexically contrastive and assigned to the first, second or third syllable within an initial three-syllable window. Stress in inflected words is determined by the stress properties of both roots and suffixes: roots are stressed or unstressed (with fixed or shifting stress across paradigms, respectively), while suffixes are stress-shifting or stress-neutral. 3543.exq_: ... suggesting that there is indeed an overarching, exceptionless rule that restricts stress to the first three syllables of the word in Choguita Rarámuri. There is indeed not a single form in the Choguita Rarámuri corpus that has stress outside this three-syllable range. (p. 167)
3543.tone: Three-way lexical tone contrast (HL 'â', L 'à', H 'á') 'exclusively realized on surface stressed syllables: there is only one lexical tone per Prosodic Word and stressless syllables lack lexical tone' (p. 44, p. 62); tone-bearing unit is the mora. The grammar treats stress and tone as phonologically independent systems of a 'hybrid' word-prosodic system (p. 133): a language with word-level stress ('stress-accent' in Hyman 2006) that also has lexical tone 'as defined for tonal languages cross-linguistically' (p. 169), under a property-driven typology that dispenses with 'pitch-accent' as a type (p. 134); stress cues are duration, onset augmentation, intensity and unstressed-vowel reduction (§5.1-5.2). Kind is lexical because a word-stress system is described; tone distribution depends on stress.

tn.quote: [p. 133] The word prosodic system of Choguita Rarámuri is complex, involving both stress and tone. ... [p. 170] The Choguita Rarámuri tone system involves a three-way lexical contrast between HL, L and H tones. The HL lexical tone is a phonological unit, a contour tone that is not decomposable into two tonal primitives. ... there is only one lexical tone per prosodic word and stressless syllables lack lexical tone ... Stressed syllables may bear any of the three lexical tones. Tone is also obligatory, i.e., there are no toneless words. The tone-bearing unit is the mora

3544.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, regardless of vowel length (syllabic trochee, 'insensible al peso'); three suffixes are extrametrical and do not count for stress placement -- absolutive -tli, agentive nominalizer -ki, and plural -tin on Spanish loans -- so stress falls on the penult of the stem before them; only one primary stress in di- and trisyllabic words. Phonetic cue is intensity (sometimes also pitch), not duration.

3544.tone: No tone. The author cites Canger (2010): 16th-17th c. Nahuatl was quantity-based with no recognised stress marking; in many modern dialects vowel-length contrast has weakened and stress is predictable on the penult. In NAHTLAX vowel-length minimal pairs are scarce and the stress cue is intensity (sometimes pitch), not duration (spectrograms Figs. 9-11).

evidence_works.detail: Dialect survey of Tlaxcala localities with a questionnaire that carried a stress variable. Finding, p. 300: 'El acento normalmente va en la penúúltima [sic] sílaba como en clásico y en la gran mayoría de los dialectos modernos.' The Malinche-slope suffix exclusion is reported second-hand: 'Los Hill (comunicación personal) comentan que en San Miguel Canoa, Pue. y en varios pueblos de las faldas de la Malinche sucede algo semejante con los sustantivos en -λi (absolutivo), -tin (plural) y -ki (agentivo). La vocal /i/ no cuenta al ponerse el acento en la antepenúltima, p. ej.: kámakλi "boca", nákastin "orejas", tepáhtiki "curandero", pero esto no sucede así si en la palabra se da -cin (rev.) o -ton (dim.): mecínλi "luna" (rev.).' (p. 300). Own Tlaxcala survey data, p. 301: 'En Tlaxcala nosotros encontramos que los sustantivos que en clásico serían de raíz bisilaba y absolutivo en -λi o -li, excepto en Ixtacuixtla, terminan en consonante y no aparece la vocal /i/:' followed by the tabulated examples tónal 'sol', λaškal 'tortilla', kóyokλ 'agujero'. Adds to the entry: (a) the -tli/-tin/-ki exclusion is reported (Hill p.c.) for San Miguel Canoa, Pue. and several villages on the Malinche slopes, not only San Isidro Buensuceso; (b) reverential -cin and diminutive -ton do not trigger it (mecínλi); (c) in the surveyed Tlaxcala localities other than Ixtacuixtla the absolutive vowel of bisyllabic-root nouns is absent (with variation for koyokλ, p. 302), so the stress of tónal, λaškal, kóyokλ falls on the penult of the consonant-final word; (d) the authors offer two historical explanations (support-vowel phonologisation vs. enclitic absolutive, pp. 301-302).

3546.prule: Each simple word carries exactly one primary stress whose position is unpredictable (lexical); the stressed syllable is the sole bearer of contrastive tone (high, low, falling), i.e. three tone-stress phonemes. All other syllables have predictable tone and predictable secondary stress or no stress.
3546.srule: Morphological constraint on the lexical placement: tone-stress sits on the first syllable of the stem or on a prefix; a stem's second syllable never bears contrastive tone-stress (§1.2, p. 243). 'sun', máhhac? 'warmed', kíppyąi? 'sap'); other non-tonic syllables have predictable tone and no stress.

3546.tone: Tone-stress system: three suprasegmental phonemes (high, low, falling glide) realised only on the single primary-stressed syllable; all other syllables have predictable tone. Gibson, Olson & Olson 1963 (Four Pame texts, Tlalocan 4(2): 125-143) revise falling to H on the first vowel of a cluster + L on the rest and add a rising tone-stress; no placement rule. 3548.prule: No rule for the Chacha language is stated. The only statement is about the present-day accent of place names attributed to Chacha: toponyms in -mal, -lap, -cat/-gat and -oc are all 'graves' (paroxytone) and this is used as a diagnostic against the -ran toponyms, which are 'agudos' (oxytone) and are therefore judged non-Chacha (probably Quechua). In the author's own phonetic corpus the Chacha-attributed names carry the accent on the monosyllabic root, i.e. the first syllable, in 10 of 11 cases ([gómal] [yúmal] [èímal] [swímal] [kúlape] [tólape]~[tólap] [ó ape] [sí gaèe] [tó gaèe] [pé gote]); the six trisyllabic forms with paragogic -e are antepenultimate, so 'graves' is only literally true of the bisyllables (or of the forms without the paragogic vowel); [osmál] is final. Initial and penultimate cannot be told apart because every Chacha toponym is a monosyllabic root + monosyllabic ending.
3548.srule: Not mentioned in Valqui Culqui 2004 (secs. 4.4, 5.1-5.5, 5.2.3, 6.1.1 read; pp. 59-69, 77-89).

Fn. 78 adds that the privative H-vs-zero system could alternatively be called an 'accent' (high pitch present vs absent), but no positional rule is given and disyllables show all four combinations (H-H, H-L, L-H, L-L, sec. 6.2.2), so it is not culminative. No word-stress position is stated anywhere in the article.

3551.tone: Two contrastive lexical tones, H (acute) vs L (unmarked), contrastive in open, glottal-final and nasal-final syllables ((78)-(80), p. 244) and in polysyllables in all combinations (6.2.1-6.2.4). Huziwara 2019 CALA (1f), in English: 'There are two contrastive tones, the high tone (marked with the acute accent) and the low tone (unmarked).' Huziwara's summary (75) of Bernot 1967 attaches intensity to individual tones (moyen-bas: 音節に若干の強勢をともなう; moyen-haut: 音節には強勢をともなう; bas: short vowel + weak final glottal stop), i.e. loudness as a tone correlate, not a positional word stress. Fn. 78's 'accent' remark is an aside about privativity; Huziwara keeps the tone analysis. Full-text search of the 2002 article for 強勢/ストレス/アクセント/卓立/プロミネンス/stress/accent gives hits only in (75) (Bernot paraphrase), fn. 78, and a Chakma reference title.
